hacker_news.title: Show HN: Pi-cowboy – use Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode as subagents
hacker_news.description: pi-cowboy is an agent orchestrator for Pi( https://pi.dev ) and Herdr( https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr ). Break large jobs into focused subtasks, hand them off to background agents running in parallel, and consolidate the results when they finish. Each agent runs in an isolated copy-on-write Git work-tree, minimising disk overhead. pi-cowboy can orchestrate foreign harnesses too, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more. Feature highlights: - Foreign harnesses: pi-cowboy agents can run in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pig and Pi-Bolt, as well as Pi. This gives you great flexibility in choosing how to spend your tokens. Running out of Codex usage? Switch your pi-cowboy harness to OpenCode, select one of its free models, and let it handle the rest. Pig and Pi-Bolt are pi variants that are more efficient, with a lower memory footprint and faster performance than pi. Because pi-cowboy is designed to run multiple agents in parallel, having a lower per-agent footprint is crucial. It prevents your machine from running out of resources and lets you have higher concurrency without choking your system. - Concurrency limits: You can configure concurrency limits at every level. Running a local model with limited resources? If a simple task already takes hours to complete, the last thing you want is to overload your machine by running too many of them at once. Set concurrency limits for that model specifically to keep resource usage under control. You can install it on Pi as a package: pi install npm:pi-cowboy #(requires `herdr` 0.8+)

hacker_news.title: Show HN: The Zelda timeline to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake
hacker_news.description: I made this ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake which comes out in 17 days. I remember the feeling of playing it as a kid but I hadn’t kept up with the story so I built a timeline to catch up before the Door of Time reopens. Nintendo’s own timeline is the authority here (Hyrule Historia and their chronicle page). The fun part was rethinking how to visualize it. It branches at the end of Ocarina into three eras depending on whether Link wins or loses, so each era is its own thread on the cloth. The threads meet again much later with Breath of the Wild. I had a lot of help from Claude. I’d often thought about building things like this but never found the time between the day job and the rest of life.

hacker_news.title: Show HN: Things to Do API
hacker_news.description: I built an api/mcp for local events: pop-ups, one-off events, concerts, etc. currently covering the SF bay area. I've been building a bunch of consumer apps lately around personalization and recommendation and have had a hard time finding this data in one spot. agents can find useful stuff through tool calls / web search, but slow. you can scrape on demand too, but i wanted a faster data set and couldn't find an existing provider for the mix of event types I was searching for. the methodology for it is to find influential accounts/posters/etc. and do a fan out across things that they co-post with. mcp: `claude mcp add --transport http thingstodo https://api.thingstodoapi.com/mcp ` I'm considering adding other cities. If you're building something that needs local event data, would something like this be useful and where would you want coverage?
